title: My England Travelogue Part 3, A Really Wonderful CFU Workshop in London op-in-london/
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov recaps a two-day London workshop on Checking for Understanding, co-facilitated with Jen Rugani, drawing out two practice-design innovations. 'Double practice' has each participant rehearse a technique twice, with a reflective pause in between to consider what they'll change or borrow, deepening metacognition about why and how one adapts a technique to context. A 'benefits and limitations' activity, applied specifically to mini-whiteboards, pushes participants past reflexive enthusiasm to honestly weigh a favourite tool's downsides -- disposability, encouraging hasty writing, and becoming a low-effort crutch that lets teachers avoid higher-risk moves like cold call. Lemov closes with two participant observations: that Do Nows can silently balloon into the whole lesson unless the error being reviewed is pre-planned, and that teachers may unconsciously ask shallower checking-for-understanding questions to avoid uncovering misconceptions they're not prepared to fix.
points: 'Double practice' -- practising a technique twice with a reflective pause in between about what to change or borrow -- was designed to build adaptive decision-making and metacognition, not just mechanical repetition.

The 'benefits and limitations' activity, applied to mini-whiteboards, surfaced real downsides even from an admitted MWB enthusiast: disposability, encouraging hasty scrawled writing, and risk of becoming 'a crutch' that lets teachers avoid higher-risk techniques.
A participant observation: Do Nows that surface unplanned misconceptions can balloon into 20-minute detours, but pre-planning the specific error to review keeps a Do Now to 5-7 minutes.

Another participant flagged a structural disincentive: substantive checking-for-understanding questions risk uncovering big misconceptions requiring 'a large fix,' which quietly nudges teachers toward asking safer, shallower questions.
quotes: The 'double' part refers to the idea that we each went twice with a bit of reflection in between.

We felt really strongly that it was worth it because it socialized participants to be attentive to adaptation: what and why and how am I changing or adapting what I am doing to the context or the question.
But a beneficial tool overused can be a liability and I must honestly say that I have seen mini-whiteboards occasionally overused.
Because they are easy and achieve a basic level of engagement, they can allow you not to use the higher risk moves of Turn and Talk or hand raising or Cold Call that a teacher would ideally also use.
If you asked really substantive questions she noted, you were likely to uncover big misconceptions or gaps in understanding. This would require a large fix and perhaps some psychological distress.
